\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over document collections increasingly works on page images as well as on
extracted text. Visual retrievers such as ColPali~\cite{colpali} embed each page as a grid of patch vectors and
score queries by late interaction~\cite{colbert}, which handles tables, charts and layouts that optical character recognition (OCR) text loses.
The price is GPU compute and memory: every query is encoded and scored against every patch vector of every page, and
a vision-language generator then reads the page image. BM25~\cite{bm25} over OCR text answers a retrieval query on a
CPU in about a millisecond for our page pools of up to 1,286 pages, but needs OCR at indexing time
(0.26 GPU-s per page with docTR, more GPU time than ColPali indexing, which processes 16.2
pages/s). A system that
answers every question through the visual path, or through both, pays for the most expensive option on every query.

\subsection{Why serving multimodal RAG is a GPU provisioning problem}
\label{sec:intro-hpc}

Three properties make serving multimodal RAG a question of how many GPUs, and which, a deployment needs, rather than
a modelling detail; routing acts on the first and the third, index placement on the second.

\emph{Compute grows with the request rate.} Generation dominates the cost of every path. Served live with vLLM on
one A10 GPU, the hybrid path alone missed a p95 latency of 2\,s even at the lowest arrival rate we tested, and at
5\,s routing sustained 1.82$\times$ its arrival rate on two GPUs (Section~\ref{sec:res-scale}).
Projected to a larger pool with a simulator driven by measured service times, which overestimated capacity by
1.4--2.0$\times$ against live serving, 100 queries/s would need 1.5$\times$
as many GPUs for the hybrid path as for content-aware routing.

\emph{Memory grows with the corpus.} ColPali stores 1,031 vectors per page; at 100k pages the index needs
24.6\,GiB in bf16, more than our 24\,GiB GPU, and a million pages (about 246\,GiB) exceed the
memory of most current accelerators. These figures are for uncompressed bf16 vectors searched exhaustively; ColBERTv2-style
residual compression~\cite{colbertv2} would need about 35\,GiB at 2 bits and 19\,GiB at 1 bit per dimension,
and binarisation about 15\,GiB (analytic sizes; their retrieval quality on this corpus is not measured here).
With exhaustive MaxSim, as measured here, such an index must be sharded, streamed from host memory or compressed;
hierarchical token pooling~\cite{tokenpooling}, evaluated here, shrinks it about fourfold with little loss of recall, and engines
such as PLAID~\cite{plaid} avoid exhaustive scoring (not evaluated here).
Exhaustive MaxSim is embarrassingly parallel over pages, so sharding it across the GPUs of a node is expected to
scale almost linearly; we measure how close it comes, and what the dispatch and merge cost, on three older
GPUs (Tesla P40) and two data-centre NVIDIA A10 GPUs (327\,ms for 50k pages on one
Tesla P40, 328\,ms for 150k pages on three). Holding the index in host memory instead, two A10s searched
a million pages in batches of 64 at 0.44\,GPU-s per query, close to GPU-resident search
(94\% of its throughput where both were measured), which would need 16 A10s; at
6.4\,s per single query, this placement suits batch rather than interactive search. Routing
does not shrink the index, since our best router reads ColPali scores for every query. The index-placement
measurements are therefore a companion characterisation of the visual tier that holds for any policy using ColPali,
not a result of routing; Table~\ref{tab:claims} lists which systems claims are measured, simulated or projected,
and at what scale.

\emph{Scope.} Every experiment in this paper runs within a single node: routing, retrieval and generation on one
GPU, live serving on up to two GPUs, and index sharding on up to three GPUs of one node. We ran no
multi-node experiment, so interconnect traffic, distributed merging of shard results and cross-node scheduling are
not measured; capacity for larger pools is a projection from the simulator, with the error stated above.

\emph{Latency targets constrain the design.} Interactive systems are judged on tail latency, so routing and
escalation should add as little serial work as possible. Our content-aware router adds 24.8\,ms of inference
before generation; we measure this overhead and charge it to every query.

Per-query routing is therefore a scheduling decision over GPU capacity: each query should get the cheapest context
that still answers it, and an operator should be able to set the trade-off between quality and capacity for a
deployment without retraining the router.

Cost-aware routing and cascades have been studied for large language models~\cite{frugalgpt,routellm}, also as one
unified framework~\cite{unifiedrouting}, and for adaptive retrieval~\cite{adaptiverag}. UniversalRAG~\cite{universalrag}
routes each query to the corpus of the right modality and granularity, and VisDoM~\cite{visdom} and
VDocRAG~\cite{vdocrag} answer questions over collections of visually rich documents, a setting introduced as
document collection visual question answering (VQA)~\cite{doccvqa}. These systems choose sources or improve answers; none charges measured
GPU cost to the choice of context; serving systems batch and schedule model inference under latency
targets~\cite{clipper,orca,vllm}, and efficient engines reduce late-interaction scoring cost~\cite{plaid}
(Section~\ref{sec:related}). We bring these threads together for multimodal document RAG, where the choice is
between context modalities that share one generator, and evaluate routing end to end on answer quality and
measured cost.
Routing, retrieval and generation are measured on a single GPU with Hugging Face (HF) Transformers generation, and capacity at
larger scale is simulated from measured service times and checked against live serving with vLLM on two A10 GPUs; multi-GPU sharding and host-memory placement of the index are
measured on two further nodes, with three older GPUs (Tesla P40) and with two NVIDIA A10 GPUs.

\subsection{Research questions}

\begin{description}
  \item[RQ1] What do the text, visual and hybrid paths cost, and how well do they answer, when measured end to end
  with real retrieval and the same generator?
  \item[RQ2] Can a router predict, before generation, which path answers a query well enough, and how close does
  it come to a per-query oracle?
  \item[RQ3] Can the cost--quality trade-off be set per deployment without retraining, and does escalating uncertain
  queries add anything beyond that setting?
  \item[RQ4] How does routing change the capacity of a GPU at a latency target, and how does the visual index scale
  with corpus size and the number of GPUs within a node?
\end{description}

\subsection{Contributions}

\begin{itemize}
  \item An end-to-end evaluation that runs every path on every query of DocVQA~\cite{docvqa} and
  InfographicVQA~\cite{infovqa} with real BM25 and ColPali retrieval and a local generator, and measures answer
  quality as average normalised Levenshtein similarity (ANLS), GPU-seconds, energy and latency per query. All tables and figures are generated from cached outputs by
  released code.
  \item Outcome-based route labels, and the finding that the keyword rule behind our earlier labels agrees with them
  no better than chance (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.01$); stronger heuristic labellers are not tested.
  \item Content-aware routing between context modalities that share one generator. The decision rule,
  $\arg\max_p \hat{q}_p - \lambda \bar{c}_p$ with $\lambda$ set per deployment, is the standard cost-penalised rule of
  routers and cascades for language models, and we make its relation to budget-constrained routing explicit. What is
  new is what the quality estimate reads and what the cost measures: CAVR-CE predicts, before any generation, how well
  each path will answer from the passages and scores that retrieval returned, and the costs are measured GPU-seconds
  of the paths themselves, not prices. Against always-hybrid it uses 29\% less GPU compute at a mean ANLS cost
  of 0.008, and the saving holds (35\%) on questions from the datasets' training splits.
  Against the best fixed policy, always-visual, it does not give a consistent gain: 0.016 ANLS for 15\%
  more compute on the design splits, not significant on the training-split questions.
  \item A serving study: capacity per GPU under Poisson load, measured live with vLLM on one and two A10 GPUs, and
  projected to larger pools by a simulator driven by measured service times, whose error against the live runs we
  report; router throughput; and visual-index latency up to 100k pages with GPU-resident, host-streamed and pooled
  placement (larger indexes built from replicated page embeddings).
  \item A characterisation of index placement within one node, independent of routing: sharding of exhaustive MaxSim
  over up to three Tesla P40 and two NVIDIA A10 GPUs, whose expected near-linear scaling we measure
  together with its dispatch and merge cost, and an index of a million pages held in host memory and streamed to
  two GPUs, compared with GPU-resident search.
\end{itemize}

We also report what does not work. With a shared generator the text path is not cheap; routing on the question text
alone is no better than always choosing the visual path; gradient boosting on the same features as CAVR-CE
matches its ANLS at a smaller saving (23\% against 29\% over always-hybrid), so the cross-encoder
adds part of the saving rather than all of it; confidence-based escalation is not an independent improvement, because
lowering $\lambda$ reaches the same operating points; a queue-driven controller for $\lambda$, evaluated in simulation under
bursty load, kept fewer requests within the latency target than a fixed, higher $\lambda$; and a per-query oracle reaches
ANLS 0.630 at 0.486 GPU-s, far beyond any router we trained, because predicting per-query success
remains hard. The path set itself is not on the cost--quality frontier: one page of OCR text is a better cheap path
than three, and three page images a better expensive path than the hybrid one (Section~\ref{sec:res-paths}).
